title: Waiting for the first success
objectives: Use the geometric distribution for the trial of the first success
Derive its mean $1/p$ by conditioning and by a series
State and use the memoryless property

screens.title: Waiting for the first success
screens.prose: You rest a limit order in the book. In any minute it fills with chance 0.2, whatever happened before. We will find how long you should expect to wait.
Each minute the order either fills or waits. Once it fills, the story stops, so only the waiting branch carries on.
screens.question: What is the chance the order first fills in minute 3?

widget.label: Chance of a first fill in minute 3

hints.text: Which path through the tree ends with a first fill in minute 3?
Wait, wait, then fill.
Multiply along the path: $0.8 \times 0.8 \times 0.2$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow the path wait, wait, fill and multiply its branches.

byKey.one-minute: 0.2 is the chance of a fill in any one minute. A first fill in minute 3 also needs two waits before it.
byKey.all-fill: $0.2^3$ asks for a fill in all three minutes. The first two minutes must be waits.
byKey.added: You added three chances of 0.2. That counts fills in different minutes as if they could all be first.
byKey.by-three: 0.488 is the chance of a fill by minute 3, $1 - 0.8^3$. You want the first fill exactly in minute 3.

explain.text: A first fill in minute 3 means the path wait, wait, fill. Its chance is $0.8 \times 0.8 \times 0.2 = 0.128$. Every extra minute of waiting adds one more factor of 0.8.

screens.prose: The bars show the chance that the first fill comes in minute $k$, for $k = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$. Slide the fill chance per minute.

derive.caption: Fill chance per minute {{fixed(p, 2)}}: first-minute fill {{fixed(p, 2)}}, still waiting after 5 minutes {{fixed(pow(1 - p, 5), 3)}}

screens.question: Which minute is the most likely one for the first fill, whatever the fill chance?

options.why: You took the average wait as the most likely one. A few very long waits pull the average out past the tallest bar.

options.text: A later minute, as the order becomes due
options.why: You expected the waiting to build up pressure. Each bar is the one before times $1 - p$, so the bars only fall.

hints.text: Look at the tallest bar as you slide.
Each bar is the previous bar times $1 - p$.

feedback.correct: Minute 1 is always the tallest bar: later minutes need extra waits first.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide the fill chance and watch which bar is tallest.

explain.text: A first fill in minute $k$ needs $k - 1$ waits first. So each bar is the one before times $1 - p$. The bars fall from minute 1 for every $p$. At $p = 1$ there is a single bar: the order always fills at once.

screens.prose: Let $X$ be the minute of the first fill. The pattern from the tree is $P(X = k) = (1 - p)^{k - 1}p$. This is the **geometric distribution**, $X \sim \text{Geo}(p)$. Here $p = 0.2$.
screens.question: What is $P(X > 3)$, the chance the order is still unfilled after 3 minutes?

hints.text: Still unfilled after 3 minutes means something about each of the first 3 minutes.
You could add every bar from minute 4 on, but there is a shortcut.
The first three minutes are all waits: $0.8^3$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. $X > 3$ means minutes 1, 2 and 3 were all waits.

byKey.complement: 0.488 is $P(X \le 3)$, the chance it has filled by then. You want the chance it has not.
byKey.off-by-one: $0.8^4$ needs four waits, which is $X > 4$. After 3 minutes only 3 waits have happened.
byKey.one-bar: 0.128 is $P(X = 3)$, one bar. $X > 3$ is every bar from 4 on.

explain.text: $X > 3$ says nothing about when the fill comes, only that minutes 1 to 3 were waits. So $P(X > 3) = 0.8^3 = 0.512$. In general $P(X > m) = (1 - p)^m$.

screens.prose: You check the order after 2 minutes. It has not filled. Every minute still fills with chance 0.2, independently.

state.caption: Given: no fill in minutes 1 and 2

screens.question: What is the chance it is still unfilled 3 minutes later, $P(X > 5 \mid X > 2)$?

options.why: That is $0.8^5 = P(X > 5)$ from the start. You already know the first two minutes were waits.
That is $0.8^2$, the chance of the two waits you already know happened.
You multiplied $0.328$ by $0.64$. Conditioning divides by $P(X > 2)$; it does not multiply.

hints.text: Use $P(A \mid B) = P(A \cap B)/P(B)$. Here $X > 5$ already implies $X > 2$.

feedback.correct: $0.8^5 / 0.8^2 = 0.8^3 = 0.512$: the same as from a fresh start.

byKey.ignore: You ignored what you saw. Two waits are already behind you, so divide by their chance.

explain.text: $P(X > 5 \mid X > 2) = 0.8^5 / 0.8^2 = 0.8^3 = 0.512$. That equals $P(X > 3)$ from the last screen. The order forgets how long it has waited: $P(X > m + n \mid X > m) = P(X > n)$, the **memoryless** property.

screens.prose: Your order has now waited 9 minutes without a fill. A colleague says it must be due: it is bound to fill soon. Nothing about the market has changed.
screens.question: What is the chance it fills in minute 10?

options.text: More than $0.2$, because it is overdue
options.why: That is the gambler's fallacy. Each minute fills with chance 0.2 whatever came before; the waits build up no pressure.

options.text: Less than $0.2$, because it looks stuck
options.why: You treated a long wait as evidence the chance has dropped. In this model each minute is independent, so the chance stays 0.2.
0.027 is $P(X = 10)$ from the start. You already know the order survived 9 minutes.

hints.text: Does the order know how long it has waited?
Divide the bar at 10 by the chance of reaching minute 10 at all.

feedback.correct: Memoryless: after any number of waits, the next minute still fills with chance 0.2.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Condition on the 9 waits you have seen.

byKey.due: You expected the waiting to make a fill due. Independent minutes have no memory, so the chance is still 0.2.

explain.text: $P(X = 10 \mid X > 9) = 0.8^9 \times 0.2 / 0.8^9 = 0.2$. A long wait does not make a fill more likely. If fills really do get likelier, the minutes are not independent and the geometric model is wrong.

screens.prose: Some software counts the failed minutes before the fill instead: $Y = X - 1$. Then $Y$ takes values $0, 1, 2, \ldots$, and $Y = 0$ means an instant fill. Same order, $p = 0.2$.

state.caption: The same bars: $X = k$ is $Y = k - 1$

screens.question: What is $P(Y = 2)$?

widget.accept: 0.128: two failed minutes, then a fill, $0.8^2 \times 0.2$
widget.label: Chance of exactly 2 failed minutes

hints.text: $Y = 2$ means two failed minutes before the fill. Which minute is the fill?
$Y = 2$ is the same event as $X = 3$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Two failures, then the fill: the fill comes in minute 3.

byKey.trials-formula: You put $k = 2$ into $(1 - p)^{k - 1}p$, the formula for trials. For failures it is $(1 - p)^k p$.
byKey.one-fill: 0.2 is one minute's fill chance. $Y = 2$ also needs two failures first.

explain.text: Counting failures shifts everything by one: $P(Y = k) = (1 - p)^k p$ and $E[Y] = E[X] - 1$. Both are called geometric. Always check which one a book or library means.

screens.prose: Now the mean wait, by conditioning on minute 1. If it fills, $X = 1$. If not, one minute is used and, by memorylessness, the wait starts afresh. So $E[X \mid \text{wait}] = 1 + E[X]$ and $$E[X] = p \cdot 1 + (1 - p)(1 + E[X]).$$
screens.question: Solve for $E[X]$ in terms of $p$.

hints.text: Expand the right-hand side.
Move $(1 - p)E[X]$ to the left: $pE[X] = 1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Expand, collect the $E[X]$ terms on the left, then divide.

byKey.p: $p$ falls as waits grow longer, so it cannot be the mean wait. Collect the $E[X]$ terms and divide by $p$.
byKey.failures: $(1 - p)/p$ is the mean number of failed minutes, $E[X] - 1$. You dropped the minute of the fill.
byKey.one-minus: You divided by $1 - p$. After collecting terms the coefficient of $E[X]$ is $p$.

explain.text: Expanding gives $E[X] = 1 + (1 - p)E[X]$, so $pE[X] = 1$ and $E[X] = 1/p$. This is the law of total expectation, split on the first minute. At $p = 0.2$ the mean wait is 5 minutes.

screens.prose: Check the mean with the series instead. Write $q = 1 - p$. By definition $E[X] = \sum_{k \ge 1} k q^{k - 1}p$.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $E[X] = pS$, where $S = 1 + 2q + 3q^2 + 4q^3 + \cdots$: take out the common factor $p$.
$S - qS = 1 + q + q^2 + q^3 + \cdots$: subtract term by term, leaving each power once.
$(1 - q)S = \dfrac{1}{1 - q}$, so $S = \dfrac{1}{p^2}$: the geometric series, with $1 - q = p$.
$E[X] = p \cdot \dfrac{1}{p^2} = \dfrac{1}{p}$: substitute back into the first line.

hints.text: Name the sum first, then find a copy of it shifted by one power.
Subtracting $qS$ from $S$ cancels the growing coefficients.
Name $S$, multiply by $q$, subtract, sum the series, substitute.

feedback.correct: The series agrees with the conditioning argument: $E[X] = 1/p$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Define $S$, shift it by one power, subtract, then sum.

byKey.end: The last line needs $S$, which the geometric series gives. Put it at the end.
byKey.sub: You can only subtract once you have both $S$ and $qS$ written out.

explain.text: Subtracting $qS$ turns coefficients $1, 2, 3, \ldots$ into $1, 1, 1, \ldots$, a plain geometric series. That sums to $1/(1 - q) = 1/p$, so $S = 1/p^2$. Two different routes give the same mean, $1/p$.

screens.prose: A researcher backtests random strategy variants with no real edge. A test at the 5% level passes by luck with chance 0.05, independently each time. Let $X$ be the number of backtests up to and including the first pass.
screens.question: On average, how many backtests until a no-edge strategy passes?

hints.text: Which distribution counts trials up to the first success?
The mean of $\text{Geo}(p)$ is $1/p$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the geometric mean, $1/p$.

byKey.failures: 19 counts the failed backtests before the pass. $X$ includes the pass itself.
byKey.percent: You read 5% as 5. The mean is $1/p = 1/0.05$.
byKey.rate: 0.05 is the chance per test. The mean wait is its reciprocal.

explain.text: The mean is $1/0.05 = 20$ backtests. Try 20 variants of nothing and, on average, one passes by luck. A pass is only meaningful once you know how many tries came before it.

screens.prose: The researcher tries only 10 no-edge variants and stops at the first pass.
screens.question: What is the chance at least one of the 10 passes by luck?

widget.label: Chance of a lucky pass in 10 tries

hints.text: Find the chance that none of the 10 pass first.
No pass in 10 tries is $X > 10$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take 1 minus the chance that all 10 fail.

byKey.added: You added 0.05 ten times. That counts runs with two passes twice; use the complement.
byKey.none: 0.5987 is $0.95^{10}$, the chance none pass. You want at least one.
byKey.tenth: 0.0315 is the chance the first pass is exactly the 10th test. Any of the 10 will do.

explain.text: None of 10 pass with chance $0.95^{10} \approx 0.5987$, so at least one passes with chance 0.4013. Ten tries of nothing give a lucky pass about two times in five. That is why a backtest count belongs in every research report.

ideas: The trial of the first success in independent trials with chance $p$ is geometric: $P(X = k) = (1 - p)^{k - 1}p$.
$P(X > m) = (1 - p)^m$, so $P(X > m + n \mid X > m) = P(X > n)$: a long wait changes nothing.
Conditioning on the first trial gives $E[X] = 1 + (1 - p)E[X]$, so $E[X] = 1/p$.

formula.name: Geometric distribution
formula.note: Counts trials, $k = 1, 2, \ldots$ Counting failures instead shifts it by 1: $E[X - 1] = (1 - p)/p$.

summary.trap: A long run of failures does not make a success due. Each trial still succeeds with chance $p$.

quiz.prose: You roll a fair die until the first six.
quiz.question: What is the chance the first six comes on roll 3?

widget.label: Chance the first six is roll 3

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Two non-sixes, then a six.

byKey.one-roll: $\tfrac{1}{6}$ is the chance of a six on any one roll. Rolls 1 and 2 must also miss.
byKey.all-six: $(\tfrac{1}{6})^3$ asks for three sixes. The first two rolls must not be sixes.

explain.text: The first six on roll 3 needs a miss, a miss, then a six. That is $(\tfrac{5}{6})^2 \times \tfrac{1}{6} = \tfrac{25}{216} \approx 0.1157$.

quiz.prose: A market order fills in the first second with chance 1. Let $X$ be the second in which it fills.
quiz.question: Which statement is true?

options.text: The geometric formula breaks down at $p = 1$
options.why: Put $p = 1$ into $(1 - p)^{k - 1}p$: you get 1 at $k = 1$ and 0 elsewhere. Nothing breaks.
With $p = 1$ there is no waiting at all. $E[X] = 1/p = 1$.

feedback.correct: At $p = 1$ the wait is certain: exactly one trial.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put $p = 1$ into the pmf and the mean.

explain.text: With $p = 1$, $P(X = 1) = 1$ and every later bar is 0. So $E[X] = 1/1 = 1$ and there is no spread. This is the edge case where nothing is random.

quiz.prose: You have rolled a fair die 4 times without a six.
quiz.question: What is the chance the next 6 rolls also have no six?

options.why: That is the chance of 10 misses from the start. The first 4 have already happened.

options.text: Less than $(\tfrac{5}{6})^6$, since a six is due
options.why: That is the gambler's fallacy. The die has no memory of the 4 misses.
You subtracted 4 from 6. The next 6 rolls are all still to come.

feedback.correct: Memoryless: the next 6 rolls behave like a fresh start.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $P(X > 10 \mid X > 4) = P(X > 6)$.

explain.text: $P(X > 10 \mid X > 4) = (\tfrac{5}{6})^{10} / (\tfrac{5}{6})^4 = (\tfrac{5}{6})^6 \approx 0.335$. The 4 misses so far do not matter. It is the same as 6 misses from a fresh start.

quiz.prose: A dealer quotes a price that each client accepts with chance 0.25, independently. Let $Y$ be the number of refusals before the first acceptance.
quiz.question: What is $E[Y]$?

feedback.correct: Trials to the first acceptance average 4, so refusals average 3.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the mean number of trials, then subtract the acceptance itself.

byKey.trials: 4 counts the quotes up to and including the acceptance. $Y$ counts only the refusals.
byKey.quarter: 0.25 is the acceptance chance. The mean wait is about its reciprocal.

explain.text: Trials to the first acceptance have mean $1/0.25 = 4$. $Y$ leaves out the acceptance, so $E[Y] = 4 - 1 = 3$. Equivalently $(1 - p)/p = 0.75/0.25 = 3$.
